keyVerseText: Ye shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead, nor print any marks upon you: I am the LORD.
rootMeaning: The root of כְּתֹבֶת (kᵉthôbeth) comes from כָּתַב (kâthab), which fundamentally means to write, inscribe, or engrave. This root conveys the idea of making a visible mark or record, often by engraving or writing on a surface. Thus, the literal sense of כְּתֹבֶת extends beyond a simple mark to imply a deliberate inscription or impression, potentially on the flesh itself, emphasizing the permanence and intentionality behind the mark.
usageInScripture: The word כְּתֹבֶת appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Leviticus 19:28, where it is translated as 'any' mark or writing on the skin. This singular occurrence highlights its specific usage referring to physical marks or inscriptions, possibly tattoos or branded signs. The consistency in translation as a mark or inscription reveals the word's narrow semantic range, focusing on visible, often bodily, impressions rather than abstract writing or documents.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding כְּתֹבֶת in its original Hebrew context enriches our grasp of biblical holiness and the call to set oneself apart from pagan practices. The prohibition against making such marks in Leviticus reflects God's desire for His people to honor their bodies as His creation, avoiding idolatrous or culturally pagan expressions of mourning or allegiance. This word reminds believers that the body is not merely a canvas for cultural expression but a temple of the Holy Spirit, to be kept pure and consecrated. Christ’s redemptive work invites us to bear His mark in our hearts rather than on our flesh, calling us to a deeper, spiritual inscription.
keyVerseReflection: Leviticus 19:28 commands, 'Ye shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead, nor print any marks upon you: I am the LORD.' Here, כְּתֹבֶת emphasizes the visible, physical nature of these forbidden marks, underscoring that God’s people are not to imitate pagan practices of mourning or idolatry through bodily inscriptions. The use of this word highlights the seriousness of maintaining holiness outwardly as well as inwardly, as a testimony to God’s sovereign lordship over His people.
